Distributed systems development faces challenges in software engineering, concurrency, distribution, and non-functional criteria.
Concurrency introduces risks like race conditions, deadlocks, and requires explicit design decisions.
Distribution involves heterogeneity, failure handling, transparency, openness, and security concerns.
Non-functional criteria include security, scalability, fault tolerance, and self-configuration.
Existing paradigms (object, component, service, agent orientation) each address some but not all distributed system challenges.
The active components approach conceptually integrates agent, service, and component paradigms.
Active components are autonomous, concurrently acting entities providing and consuming services.
Jadex middleware implements active components with support for component management and communication.
Active components enable concurrency control by hiding concurrency details while ensuring consistency.
Distribution transparency is achieved by allowing active components to interact via local or remote services transparently.
Openness is supported through clear interfaces and dynamic composition of active components.
Scalability is addressed by replication and distribution of critical components.
Failure handling in distributed systems is more complex than in single systems due to network partitions and node breakdowns.
The paper includes real-world applications such as chat systems to demonstrate the approach.
Active components support dynamic reconfiguration and self-adaptation to changing environments.
Middleware setup and configuration are critical for managing distributed applications.
The paper categorizes distributed system characteristics into concurrency, distribution, non-functional, and software engineering criteria.
Concurrency can be explicitly represented at design and implementation phases to better manage parallelism.
Security in distributed systems requires authentication, confidentiality, and protection against tampering.
The active components approach aims to provide an intuitive, unified model for distributed systems development.
